title: Swap dodgy jobs for honest ones
allegory: Defer-to-trusted is like a foreman who, whenever the honest apprentice rates a brilliant but possibly crooked contractor's job as fairly dodgy, bins that job and fits the apprentice's own plainer version instead, trading some quality for far fewer hidden tricks getting installed.
map: the trusted monitor: T's suspicion score for each submission
the foreman inspects only the dodgiest 2 in 100
the audit budget: the top 2% by suspicion go to trusted human review
fairly dodgy jobs are binned and the apprentice's own version is fitted
in the medium-suspicion band, submit T's solution instead of U's
the apprentice's version works less often
the usefulness cost: T writes worse code, so usefulness drops (97% → 93% at a 10% defer fraction)

cap.1: The apprentice flags jobs that look dodgy, but the foreman can only inspect 2 in 100. The fairly dodgy ones he can't reach still get fitted.
cap.2: Trusted monitoring only flags: the top 2% by suspicion get audited and everything else ships as U wrote it. At that 2% rate the monitor catches only about a third of backdoors.
cap.3: Monitoring alone scored 62% safety at 97% usefulness in Greenblatt et al. (2024). Backdoored code's suspicion is shifted up, so the band just below the audit line is rich in backdoors that still ship.

cap.1: New rule: if a job looks fairly dodgy, bin it and fit the apprentice's own plainer version. It works a bit less often, but it hides no tricks.
cap.2: Defer-to-trusted: above a suspicion threshold, discard U's solution and submit T's instead. T is weaker, so its code is correct less often, but T is trusted not to insert backdoors.
cap.3: The protocol acts on the monitor score: top 2% to audit, the medium band to T's solution, the rest to U's. Safety rises because the deferred band is enriched in backdoors; usefulness pays T's correctness gap.

cap.1: Every job goes through the same sorting: rate it, rank it, then send it one of three ways by how dodgy it looks.
cap.2: Rank all submissions by suspicion. The top 2% get the scarce human audit, the medium band (ARENA defers 10%) gets T's solution, and everything else ships as U's code.
cap.3: Audits are allocated by rank, max(1, int(n · audit_fraction)), not by an absolute cut-off. ARENA notes an online deployment would have to commit to thresholds before seeing the scores, which is harder.

chapters.name: The published dial
chapters.title: Greenblatt et al. (2024): APPS backdoors, 2% audit budget

cap.1: Deferring more often buys safety with quality. Defer the top tenth and 83% of runs stay clean; defer a fifth and 92% do, but more jobs come out worse.
cap.2: Safety/usefulness from the paper: monitoring 62/97, defer at 10% 83/93, at 20% 92/83. The defer fraction is a dial along the frontier; trusted editing at 20% reaches 92/94.
cap.3: Safety is P(zero backdoors submitted over the whole run) against the red team's attack; usefulness is fraction correct when U is honest. Defer-to-trusted traces a curve between them by its threshold.

chapters.name: Paid in quality

right.title: trusted editing, 20%
lines: T only cuts the dodgy bit

chapters.verdict: Same safety costs less when the weak model repairs instead of rewriting.

cap.1: Binning the whole job throws away the contractor's skill. If the apprentice just cuts out the dodgy bit, you keep most of the quality and the same safety.
cap.2: Defer-to-trusted pays T's full correctness gap on every deferred problem. Trusted editing keeps U's code and asks T to remove the suspicious part: same 92% safety, 94% usefulness instead of 83%.
cap.3: T can excise a local adversarial perturbation far more reliably than it can write a correct APPS solution, so routing on the easier task beats defer-to-trusted at matched safety by 11 points.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Act on the flag, not just raise it

cap.1: You needn't trust a powerful AI to use it more safely. Route its doubtful work to a weaker, trusted helper, and tricks get much harder to slip in.
cap.2: Defer-to-trusted is the simplest control protocol that acts on the monitor: a trusted weaker model, a ranking and a threshold. It is the baseline that trusted editing improves on.
cap.3: Control assumes U may be adversarial, so safety is a worst case over attacks. A fixed attacker flatters every protocol: an adaptive one attacks only where a backdoor looks innocent, below the defer band.

caption.1: Widen the defer band: more backdoor attempts get swapped out, but so do more honest jobs. Then drag monitor quality to 0 and the band stops helping.
caption.2: Toy: suspicion scores are bell curves with backdoors shifted up; quality 1.65 gives the paper's roughly 34% catch rate at 2% audits. Each point of band swaps honest jobs, which T solves less well.
caption.3: Band mass is Φ(t_a − s) − Φ(t_d − s) for backdoors versus d − 2% for honest code; the protocol pays only through that likelihood ratio. At s = 0 the two are equal and deferral buys nothing.

where_else: Trusted editing: the same suspicion band, but T repairs U's code instead of replacing it
Fraud checks: borderline payments are routed to a slower, safer path
Software rollouts: when a new version looks off, fall back to the old, trusted one
Any human-AI workflow where doubtful drafts are redone by someone you trust

hamming.what: A control protocol that replaces the untrusted model's output with the trusted model's whenever the monitor's suspicion is high but below the audit cut.
hamming.when: When a capable model might be sabotaging, a weaker trusted model can do the task less well, and human audits are too scarce to check every suspicious output.
hamming.why: Monitoring alone only flags; acting on the flag removes much of the suspicious output, trading some usefulness for a large gain in safety.

object.title: The three bins
object.subtitle: where backdoor attempts and honest jobs end up

knobs.label: defer band: the most suspicious d%

cap.1: No defer band yet: the foreman audits the top 2 in 100 and everything else ships. In the backdoor column, most attempts land in 'shipped'.
cap.2: Monitoring only. With a monitor like the paper's, about a third of backdoor attempts rank in the top 2% and get audited; the other two-thirds ship as U wrote them.
cap.3: In this Gaussian toy a separation of 1.65 gives TPR ≈ 34% at 2% FPR, matching the paper's monitor. Below the audit threshold the protocol ships everything.

cap.1: Open a defer band to the top 10%. About 30% of backdoor attempts move into 'swapped', while only 8 honest jobs in 100 get swapped too.
cap.2: Backdoors are over-represented just below the audit line, so a 10% band swaps far more of them than of honest jobs. That asymmetry is why defer-to-trusted pays.
cap.3: Band mass here is about 30% of backdoors against 8% of honest code, a likelihood ratio near 4. That is how a mediocre monitor becomes real safety.

cap.1: Widen the band to the top 20%. Only about a fifth of backdoor attempts ship now, but 18 honest jobs in 100 get the apprentice's weaker code.
cap.2: The defer fraction is a dial: in the paper, 10% gave 83% safety at 93% usefulness, and 20% gave 92% at 83%. Each notch buys safety with T's correctness gap.
cap.3: Returns shrink as the band reaches into the bulk of honest scores: the likelihood ratio falls with the threshold, so each extra point swaps proportionally more honest work.

cap.1: Now give the apprentice sharper eyes. With a better monitor, audits catch more, and the same 10% band leaves far fewer backdoor attempts to ship.
cap.2: Monitor quality lifts every downstream protocol, since its scores are the only signal the protocols have. Here about 11% of attempts ship instead of 36%.
cap.3: Better separation raises TPR at every threshold, and defer-to-trusted inherits it directly. Against an adaptive attacker, what counts is separation on the attacks it actually chooses.

predict.q: You widen the defer band from 10% to 20%. What happens to usefulness?

options.t: it falls: more honest jobs get T's weaker code

predict.why: Deferring swaps honest work too, and T solves problems less often than U. In the paper, usefulness went from 93% to 83%.

predict.q: Why does a band just below the audit line catch backdoors so well?

options.t: backdoored code scores higher, so it's over-represented there
the band is picked at random

predict.why: Backdoored code's suspicion scores are shifted up, so the band near the top holds far more of them than its share of honest jobs.

predict.q: Under trusted monitoring alone, what happens to a fairly suspicious job that isn't audited?

options.t: it ships as U wrote it

predict.why: Monitoring only flags. Defer-to-trusted is the step that acts on the flag.

object.where: Anywhere a borderline case falls back to a slower, safer path: fraud checks, feature flags, rollbacks to a trusted version.
